back: Merge joins two branches with a merge commit and keeps the real history. Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, rewriting them into a linear history. Never rebase commits others have already pulled.

front: What is a Git commit, really?
back: A snapshot of the whole tree plus metadata (author, message) and a pointer to its parent commit(s). Branches are just movable pointers to commits; history is a graph (DAG).
Everyone integrates small changes into main frequently (at least daily) through short-lived branches, kept releasable by CI and feature flags. The opposite of long-lived feature branches.
A commit message format: type(scope): subject, e.g. feat:, fix:, chore:, docs:, refactor:, test:. It makes history readable and enables automated changelogs and semver bumps.

JS runs on one thread with a call stack. Async work (timers, I/O) is handed to the runtime; when it finishes, its callback is queued. When the stack is empty, the loop runs all microtasks (promises) first, then the next macrotask (timer, I/O callback).

Microtasks (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) run right after the current task, all of them, before rendering or the next macrotask. Macrotasks are setTimeout, setInterval, I/O callbacks. So Promise.then runs before setTimeout(fn, 0).
Both accept any value. `any` turns off type checking entirely. `unknown` forces you to narrow (typeof, instanceof, a Zod parse) before using it. Prefer `unknown` for untrusted data.

Types are erased at compile time, so they can't check data arriving at runtime (requests, JSON, env vars). You need a runtime validator like Zod at the boundaries; z.infer gives you the static type from the same schema.

front: What does TypeScript strict mode enable?
back: strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, strictPropertyInitialization, and more. Most importantly, null and undefined are no longer assignable to every type.

A monolith is one deployable unit: simple, fast in-process calls, real transactions. Microservices deploy and scale independently but add network failures, distributed data and operational cost. Start with a modular monolith and extract services only when there's a clear reason.
One deployable app split internally into modules with explicit boundaries: each owns its data and exposes a public interface. You get monolith simplicity with a clean path to extract services later.
An API style built around resources identified by URLs, manipulated with standard HTTP methods, stateless requests, and representations like JSON. Status codes communicate the result.
PUT replaces the whole resource with the body you send (idempotent). PATCH applies a partial update; it is not guaranteed idempotent (e.g. 'increment by 1').
GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS (and TRACE). POST and PATCH are not by default. Idempotent means repeating the request has the same effect as doing it once.
Safe methods don't change server state (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS). Idempotent methods may change state, but repeating them changes nothing further (PUT, DELETE). All safe methods are idempotent.
401: not authenticated (who are you?). 403: authenticated but not allowed. 404: not found, which is also used instead of 403 to avoid revealing that a private resource exists.
400: malformed request (bad JSON, wrong types). 422: well-formed but fails validation rules. 409: conflicts with the current state (duplicate, version mismatch).
Problem Details for HTTP APIs: a standard JSON error body with type, title, status, detail and instance, served as application/problem+json.

Offset (LIMIT/OFFSET) is simple but slow on deep pages and skips or duplicates rows when data changes. A cursor (WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n) uses an index, stays fast and is stable under inserts.
INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row of the left table, with NULLs where the right table has no match.

front: Query: users who studied every day this week.
back: SELECT user_id FROM reviews WHERE reviewed_at >= date_trunc('week', now()) GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT reviewed_at::date) = (current_date - date_trunc('week', now())::date + 1). Convert to the user's time zone before taking ::date.

Finding runs of consecutive values (e.g. study streaks). Trick: for each distinct day, day - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY day) is constant within a run, so GROUP BY that difference to get each island and its length.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregates like COUNT(*).
A group of statements that succeed or fail together. In Rehearse: inserting a review and updating card_states must happen together, or neither.
Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: constraints always hold. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work. Durability: once committed, it survives a crash.

front: What are the SQL isolation levels?
back: Read uncommitted, read committed (Postgres default), repeatable read, serializable. Higher levels prevent more anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms) at the cost of more conflicts and retries.

front: How would you index the study queue query?
back: A composite index on card_states(user_id, due_at): equality column first, then the range/sort column. The query WHERE user_id = $1 AND due_at <= now() ORDER BY due_at becomes one index range scan.

front: Why does column order in a composite index matter?
back: A B-tree index sorts by the first column, then the second within it. It can serve queries on a leftmost prefix. Put equality filters first, then range or sort columns.

front: What is an N+1 query problem?
back: Loading a list with one query, then running one more query per item. Fix it with a JOIN, WHERE id IN (...), or a batching loader.
It runs the query and shows the actual plan: scan types (seq vs index), row estimates vs actual rows, and time per node. Use it to confirm an index is used.

front: What happens when you type a URL in the browser?
back: DNS resolves the host to an IP; TCP connection (plus TLS handshake for HTTPS); the browser sends an HTTP request; the server responds; the browser parses HTML, fetches CSS/JS/images, builds the DOM and CSSOM, lays out and paints.

front: How does SM-2 spaced repetition work?
back: Each card has an ease factor, interval and repetition count. A good rating multiplies the interval by the ease (1 day, 6 days, then interval × ease); a failed rating resets reps and the interval. Ease goes up or down with answer quality, never below 1.3.
A state change in the component, its parent re-rendering, or a change in a context it consumes. Props changing is a consequence of the parent re-rendering.

front: How do you find unnecessary re-renders?
back: React DevTools Profiler ('highlight updates' and the flame chart showing why each component rendered). Fix with better state placement, memo, useMemo/useCallback, or splitting context.

front: When should you NOT use useEffect?
back: For deriving data from props or state (compute it during render), for handling user events (do it in the handler), or to reset state on prop change (use a key). Effects are for syncing with external systems.

useState suits simple independent values. useReducer suits state with several related fields or transitions that depend on the previous state, like a study session state machine. It also centralizes and tests the update logic.

front: How do you prevent XSS when rendering user content?
back: Render it as text (React escapes by default), never with dangerouslySetInnerHTML on raw input. If HTML or Markdown is needed, sanitize with an allowlist (DOMPurify). Add a Content Security Policy as defense in depth.

front: What is a Content Security Policy?
back: An HTTP header telling the browser which sources may load scripts, styles, images and so on. It blocks inline scripts and unknown origins, limiting the damage of XSS.

front: How do you make a keyboard-driven app accessible?
back: Use native elements (button, not div), a visible focus indicator, logical tab order, documented shortcuts that don't clash with screen readers, ARIA only where native semantics fall short, and announce dynamic changes with aria-live.

front: How do you handle plurals in i18n?
back: Don't concatenate count + 's'. Use ICU MessageFormat or Intl.PluralRules: languages have different plural categories (one, few, many, other), and the translator writes each form.
Managing server state: caching, deduplicating requests, background refetching, retries, and optimistic updates. It separates server state from local UI state.
Authentication proves who you are (login). Authorization decides what you're allowed to do (can this user edit this deck?).
Never in plain text or with a fast hash. Use a slow, salted password hash: Argon2id (preferred), bcrypt or scrypt, tuned so one hash takes about 100 ms.
A random value unique per password, stored next to the hash. It makes identical passwords hash differently and defeats precomputed rainbow tables.

A session is a random ID pointing to server-side state: easy to revoke. A JWT is a signed, self-contained token: no lookup, but hard to revoke before it expires. For a single web app, sessions in an httpOnly cookie are usually simpler and safer.

front: Where would you store a JWT in the browser?
back: In an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, so JavaScript (and XSS) can't read it. localStorage is readable by any injected script.

The app redirects the user to the provider; the user consents; the provider redirects back with a short-lived code; the app's server exchanges the code (plus its secret) for tokens. The tokens never pass through the browser URL.

Proof Key for Code Exchange: the client sends a hash of a random verifier with the auth request and the verifier itself when exchanging the code. A stolen authorization code is useless without the verifier.

front: What is IDOR and how do you prevent it?
back: Insecure Direct Object Reference: changing an ID in a URL to access someone else's data. Prevent it by checking ownership on every query (WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $user), return 404, and test every endpoint for it.
RBAC grants permissions by role (admin, member). ABAC decides from attributes of the user, resource and context (owner, deck visibility, time). RBAC is simpler; ABAC is more flexible.
A browser rule: a page may only read responses from another origin if that server allows it with Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers. It protects users; it is not server-side access control.

front: Why does a CORS preflight happen?
back: For non-simple requests (methods like PUT/DELETE, custom headers, JSON content type), the browser first sends an OPTIONS request to ask whether the real request is allowed.

front: What is CSRF and how do you prevent it?
back: Cross-Site Request Forgery: another site makes the user's browser send an authenticated request using their cookies. Prevent it with SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens, and checking the Origin header.
Broken access control, cryptographic failures, injection (SQL, XSS), insecure design, security misconfiguration, vulnerable components, authentication failures, SSRF.

Single responsibility; Open/closed (extend without modifying); Liskov substitution (subtypes work wherever the base type does); Interface segregation (small, focused interfaces); Dependency inversion (depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations).
Passing a component its dependencies instead of having it create them. It makes code testable and swappable, e.g. passing a database repository or a clock into a service.
Code that calls Date.now() directly is hard to test (due dates, streaks, time zones). Injecting a clock lets tests set any time deterministically.
Strategy: interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, chosen at runtime (SM-2 vs FSRS). Factory: encapsulates which concrete object to create. A factory often picks which strategy to use.

Instead of fixed examples, you state properties that must hold for all inputs, and the tool (fast-check) generates hundreds of random inputs and shrinks failures to a minimal case. Example: the SRS interval is never negative; a rating of 'again' always lowers or resets it.

front: What do you test and what don't you test?
back: Test business logic, edge cases, boundaries, and bugs you've fixed. Don't test framework or library internals, trivial getters, or implementation details that make tests break on harmless refactors.
Stub: returns canned answers. Mock: also verifies how it was called. Fake: a working lightweight implementation (in-memory repository). Fakes produce less brittle tests than mocks.

front: How do you fix a flaky test?
back: Reproduce it (run it in a loop), then find the nondeterminism: time, random values, ordering, shared state, real network, race conditions. Fix the cause (inject the clock, isolate data, await properly); never just add retries.
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, few slow end-to-end tests. The higher up, the more confidence per test but more cost and flakiness.

front: How would you design uploads of large files?
back: The client asks the API for a presigned URL and uploads directly to S3 (multipart for large files), then tells the API it's done. The API never streams the bytes, so it stays fast and cheap.
A URL signed with your credentials that grants temporary, specific access (e.g. PUT one object key for 5 minutes) without exposing credentials.

front: Why not store files in the database?
back: They bloat the database, backups and replication, they're slow to stream, and DB storage is far more expensive than object storage. Store files in S3 and keep the key and metadata in the database.

front: How do you secure user files in S3?
back: Block all public access, use per-user key prefixes, give access only through short-lived presigned URLs generated after an authorization check, and encrypt at rest.

front: What is a state machine and why model status that way?
back: A fixed set of states and allowed transitions (pending → uploaded → transcribing → done | failed). It makes invalid states impossible and every transition explicit and testable.

front: How do you estimate storage cost?
back: Users × items per user × average size × price per GB-month, plus requests and egress. Example: 1,000 users × 50 recordings × 1 MB = 50 GB ≈ $1.15/month on S3 Standard.
To take slow or unreliable work out of the request path, absorb traffic spikes, retry failures, and let producers and consumers scale independently.
A message is guaranteed to be processed, but may be delivered more than once (e.g. a worker crashes after doing the work but before acknowledging). Consumers must be idempotent.

front: How do you make a job idempotent?
back: Give it a unique key and record completion (e.g. a unique constraint or 'already processed' row) in the same transaction as its effect; check before calling external APIs, and pass idempotency keys to them.
Retry after delays that grow exponentially (1s, 2s, 4s...) up to a cap, plus a random component. Jitter stops many clients from retrying at the same instant and overwhelming a recovering service.

front: Token bucket vs sliding window rate limiting?
back: Token bucket: tokens refill at a fixed rate, each request spends one; allows short bursts. Sliding window: counts requests in the last N seconds; smoother, no burst at window edges. Return 429 with Retry-After.

front: How would you build a real-time leaderboard?
back: A Redis sorted set: ZINCRBY to add points, ZREVRANGE for the top N, ZREVRANK for a user's rank, all O(log n). Persist scores to Postgres as the source of truth.
The app reads the cache; on a miss, it reads the database and writes the result into the cache with a TTL. On writes, update the database and delete the cache key.

When a hot key expires, many requests miss at once and all hit the database. Prevent it with a lock so one request rebuilds the value, early probabilistic refresh, or serving stale data while refreshing.
You must know every cached value affected by a write, and races between a read repopulating the cache and a write deleting it can leave stale data. TTLs bound how long staleness lasts.

A VM virtualizes hardware and runs its own kernel: strong isolation, heavier. A container shares the host kernel and isolates processes with namespaces and cgroups: lightweight, starts in milliseconds.

front: How do you make Docker images smaller?
back: Multi-stage builds, slim or distroless base images, install only production dependencies, a .dockerignore, and combine layers. Order layers from least to most frequently changed for caching.

front: How does Docker layer caching work?
back: Each instruction creates a layer. If an instruction and its inputs haven't changed, the cached layer is reused. Copy package.json and install dependencies before copying source code.

On every PR: install, lint, typecheck, test, build. Merges to main are blocked unless it passes. On merge: build an image, push to a registry, deploy to staging, run smoke tests, then promote to production.

Blue/green: run the new version alongside the old and switch all traffic at once; instant rollback. Canary: send a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, and ramp up gradually.

front: How do you rename a column with zero downtime?
back: Expand and contract: add the new column, write to both, backfill, switch reads to the new column, stop writing the old one, then drop it — each step its own deploy.

front: What happens to a running job when a container is stopped?
back: It receives SIGTERM and a grace period, then SIGKILL. Handle SIGTERM: stop taking new jobs, finish or release the current one. Jobs must also be idempotent in case they're killed anyway.

front: Walk me through deploying the app to AWS.
back: Images in ECR; ECS Fargate services for api and worker behind an Application Load Balancer; Postgres and Redis managed; S3 + CloudFront for files and the frontend; secrets in Secrets Manager; everything defined in Terraform and deployed by GitHub Actions.
Lambda: per-request billing, scales to zero, great for spiky or event-driven work, but has time limits and cold starts. Containers: steady load, long-running processes, WebSockets, full control.
The delay when a serverless platform must create a new execution environment (download code, start the runtime, run init) before handling a request.

front: How do you auto-scale background workers?
back: Scale on queue depth or the age of the oldest message, not CPU: add workers when the backlog grows, remove them when it drains, with min and max limits.

front: What is Terraform state and why lock it?
back: State maps your configuration to real resources. Store it remotely (S3) and lock it so two applies can't run at once and corrupt it or create duplicates.

front: The AWS bill tripled. How do you investigate?
back: Cost Explorer grouped by service, then by usage type and tag; find what changed and when; correlate with deploys. Usual suspects: NAT gateway data, egress, forgotten resources, logs, a runaway loop. Then add budgets and alerts.

front: How do you price an AI feature so it's profitable?
back: Measure the cost per use (tokens, transcription minutes), estimate usage per user (heavy users matter most), and price above that with margin, often with usage limits or credits so heavy users can't make you lose money.

front: How do you handle Stripe webhooks reliably?
back: Verify the signature, store the event ID with a unique constraint to ignore duplicates, return 2xx quickly and process asynchronously, and don't rely on event order; fetch the latest object state if needed.

front: Why a ledger instead of a balance column?
back: An append-only ledger records every credit and debit with its reason, so the balance is auditable, reproducible and easy to debug. A balance column loses history and is easy to corrupt under concurrency.

front: How do you prevent spending the same credit twice?
back: Do the balance check and the debit atomically: a transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the account, or a conditional update (UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= cost), with constraints that forbid negative balances.
A unique key the client sends with a request. The server stores the key with the result; a retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of repeating the action.

Write the business change and an 'event to publish' row in the same database transaction; a separate process reads the outbox and publishes to the queue. No lost or phantom events when one of the two writes would fail.
A boundary in DDD within which a model and its terms have one meaning. 'Card' means something different in Study than in Billing; each context owns its own model.

front: What is an aggregate in DDD?
back: A cluster of objects treated as one unit for changes, with a root that enforces invariants. All changes go through the root, in one transaction (e.g. a CreditAccount and its ledger entries).

front: How would you design usage-based billing?
back: Meter usage events idempotently, reserve credits before expensive work, capture on success, release on failure, record everything in a ledger, and reconcile against the payment provider.

front: How do you debug something that only happens in production?
back: Use logs, traces and metrics to narrow it down (which users, which version, when it started), compare with recent changes, reproduce with production-like data or config, and add targeted logging if needed.

Logs: detailed events. Metrics: cheap numeric aggregates over time, used for dashboards and alerts. Traces: the path and timing of one request across services. Together they're the three pillars of observability.

front: How do you trace a request through a message queue?
back: Propagate the trace context (W3C traceparent) in message metadata; the consumer continues the trace from it, so one trace shows the request, queue wait and job processing.

front: What is an SLO for a background job?
back: A target like '99% of transcription jobs finish within 2 minutes over 30 days', measured from enqueue to completion. The error budget is the 1% you can miss.
SLI: the measured indicator (latency, success rate). SLO: the internal target for it. SLA: a contract with customers that has consequences, usually looser than the SLO.
After repeated failures to a dependency, stop calling it for a while (open), fail fast or fall back, then let a test request through (half-open) to check whether it has recovered.
Isolating resources (connection pools, workers, queues) per dependency or feature so a failure in one can't exhaust resources for the others — e.g. LLM grading can't starve flashcard studying.
A write-up after an incident: timeline, impact, root causes, what went well, and action items. It focuses on systems and processes, not who to blame, so people share what actually happened.

front: How would you scale this database to 100x?
back: Measure first; fix slow queries and indexes; add connection pooling; cache hot reads; add read replicas; partition big tables; archive old data; shard only as a last resort.

front: What is table partitioning? When does it hurt?
back: Splitting a big table into smaller ones by a key (e.g. reviews by month). It helps when queries filter by that key and for dropping old data. It hurts when queries don't include the partition key, so they scan every partition.
Two transactions read the same value, both modify it, and the second write silently overwrites the first, e.g. reviewing the same card on two devices.

Pessimistic: lock the row first (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), others wait. Optimistic: no lock; include a version column and UPDATE ... WHERE version = $old; if 0 rows change, retry. Optimistic suits low contention.

front: How do you scale WebSockets across servers?
back: Use a load balancer that supports WebSockets and a pub/sub layer (Redis) so a message published on one server reaches clients connected to other servers. Store room state outside the server process.

front: How do you stop cheating in a real-time quiz game?
back: The server is authoritative: it keeps the answers, validates timing using server time, scores answers itself, and rate-limits. Never trust the client's score or clock.
During a network partition, a distributed system must choose consistency (refuse some requests) or availability (answer with possibly stale data). Without partitions you can have both.

front: How would you build an AI feature that grades answers?
back: Send the question, the reference answer and the user's answer to an LLM with a rubric, request structured output (score + feedback), run it in a background job, and validate the output. Measure accuracy against human grades with evals.
A test set of inputs with expected outputs or human grades used to measure an LLM feature's quality. Run them on every prompt or model change to catch regressions.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation: embed documents, store the vectors, embed the user's query, retrieve the most similar chunks, and include them in the prompt so the model answers from real sources.
Ground answers in retrieved sources, ask the model to cite them or say 'I don't know', use structured outputs, lower the temperature, and verify with evals.

Untrusted input containing instructions that hijack the model ('ignore previous instructions...'). Defend by separating instructions from data, limiting what tools the model can use, validating outputs, and never giving it secrets or unchecked actions.

front: How do you control LLM cost and latency?
back: Smaller models where quality allows, shorter prompts, prompt caching, batching, streaming responses, caching repeated results, max token limits, and per-user quotas.
The model returns a structured request to call a function you defined (name + arguments); your code runs it and sends the result back, so the model can act on real data.

front: What makes an AI agent risky?
back: It takes actions in a loop with real tools, so mistakes or prompt injection can do real damage. Limit its permissions, require confirmation for irreversible actions, set step and cost limits, and log everything.

front: How would you design an online code judge?
back: The API stores the submission and enqueues it; isolated runners execute the code against test cases with time and memory limits; the results are stored and pushed to the client.

front: How do you safely run untrusted code?
back: Isolate it: a separate container or microVM with no network, a read-only filesystem, a non-root user, CPU/memory/process limits (cgroups), a seccomp profile, a timeout, an output size limit, and no secrets in the environment.

Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel exploit can escape. MicroVMs (Firecracker, gVisor-style sandboxes) give each workload its own kernel boundary with near-container startup times. Use microVMs for hostile code.

front: What is a fork bomb and how do you stop it?
back: A process that endlessly copies itself until the system runs out of processes or memory. Stop it with a process limit (cgroups pids.max, ulimit -u) and memory limits.

front: What is the cloud metadata endpoint and why block it?
back: 169.254.169.254 serves instance info and temporary cloud credentials. Untrusted code or an SSRF that reaches it can steal those credentials, so block it from sandboxes (and use IMDSv2).
A binary tree stored in an array where every parent is ≤ its children, so the minimum is at the root. Insert and remove-min are O(log n), peek is O(1). Children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2.

front: How would you make a web app work offline?
back: A service worker caches the app shell and assets; data lives in IndexedDB; user actions are written to a local queue and synced when back online, with conflict resolution.

front: How do you resolve sync conflicts?
back: Options: last-write-wins (simple, loses data), merge per field, or sync an append-only log of events (like reviews) and recompute state, which avoids most conflicts.
A script that runs in the background, separate from the page, and can intercept network requests. It enables offline caching, background sync and push notifications.
Cache first (static assets), network first with cache fallback (fresh data), and stale-while-revalidate (serve cache, update in the background).

front: A user asks to delete all their data. What does that involve?
back: Delete or anonymize it everywhere: database rows, files in S3, embeddings, caches, analytics, logs where feasible, and third-party processors; handle backups by expiry; confirm and keep a record of the request.

front: What metrics would you track for a learning app?
back: Activation (first study session completed), DAU/WAU, retention cohorts (day 1, 7, 30), streak length, reviews per session, and the conversion rate from free to paid.

front: What is activation? What is retention?
back: Activation: the moment a new user first gets real value (e.g. finishes their first session). Retention: the share of users who come back after N days or weeks.

front: How do you run a fair A/B test?
back: Pick one primary metric and the sample size beforehand, randomize by user, run for the planned duration without peeking and stopping early, check for sample ratio mismatch, then compare with a statistical test.

front: Pod vs Deployment vs Service in Kubernetes?
back: Pod: one or more containers scheduled together. Deployment: keeps N replicas of a pod running and handles rolling updates. Service: a stable network address and load balancing for a set of pods.

front: System design: how do you structure a 45-minute interview?
back: Requirements (functional and non-functional) → back-of-the-envelope estimates → API and data model → high-level design → deep dives → bottlenecks and trade-offs.

front: Design a URL shortener: key points?
back: Generate a short unique ID (base62 counter or random with a collision check), store id → URL, redirect with 301/302, cache hot links, and it's read-heavy, so scale reads with caching and replicas.

front: How do you explain a technical trade-off to a business person?
back: Frame it in their terms: cost, risk, time and user impact. Give 2–3 options with consequences and a recommendation, e.g. 'Grading costs X per answer; this plan loses money on heavy users, so I added credits.'

front: Tell me about a time you said no to a feature.
back: STAR: the situation and the request, why you declined (cost, scope, the users it would serve), how you explained it, and what you did instead.
It translates domain names into IP addresses through a hierarchy: resolver → root → TLD → authoritative server, with caching at every level controlled by TTLs.
TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, with flow and congestion control (HTTP/1, HTTP/2). UDP: connectionless, no guarantees, lower overhead (DNS, video, QUIC/HTTP/3).

front: What happens in a TLS handshake?
back: Client and server agree on a version and cipher, the server proves its identity with a certificate, and they derive shared session keys (ECDHE). TLS 1.3 does it in one round trip.
HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection with header compression. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP), removing TCP head-of-line blocking and making handshakes faster.
L4 routes by IP and port (TCP/UDP), fast and protocol-agnostic. L7 understands HTTP and can route by path, header or cookie, terminate TLS, and do retries.
A process has its own memory space. Threads are units of execution inside a process that share its memory: cheaper, but they need synchronization.

front: What are Unix signals? SIGTERM vs SIGKILL?
back: Asynchronous notifications sent to a process. SIGTERM asks it to shut down and can be handled; SIGKILL kills immediately and can't be caught.

front: What do Unix file permissions like 755 mean?
back: Three digits for owner, group and others; each is read (4) + write (2) + execute (1). 755: the owner can read, write and execute; everyone else can read and execute.
